meta.descSnooker: Play snooker free in 3D: a full 15-red frame or a quick 6-red game against the computer, a friend or solo, with real scoring and fouls, cue ball spin, long-pot and clearance drills and an aim line you can switch off.

snooker.name: Snooker
snooker.blurb: Full 3D snooker frames with fouls, breaks and practice drills.

snooker.q1: How do you play snooker here?
snooker.a1: Press Play and start from the D. Drag on the table to aim (in top view the cue points where you touch; behind the ball, drag sideways), set the power with the slider, tap the cue ball picture for draw, follow or side, and press Shoot. On a keyboard, ← and → turn (Shift for fine turns), ↑ and ↓ change the power, Space shoots and C switches the camera.
snooker.q2: What are the rules of snooker?
snooker.a2: There are 15 reds and six colours. You must pot a red first, then any colour, then a red again, for as long as you keep potting; that run is your break. Colours potted while reds remain come back to their spots. When the reds are gone, the colours are taken in order: yellow, green, brown, blue, pink and black. The player with more points when the black goes down wins the frame.
snooker.q3: How many points is each ball worth?
snooker.a3: A red is 1, yellow 2, green 3, brown 4, blue 5, pink 6 and black 7. Taking every red with the black and then clearing the colours gives the maximum break of 147. In 6-red snooker the maximum is 75.
snooker.q4: What is a foul in snooker?
snooker.a4: Missing every ball, hitting a ball that is not on first, potting a ball that is not on, or putting the cue ball in a pocket (an in-off). A foul gives your opponent 4 points, or the value of the ball involved if that is higher, up to 7, and ends your turn. After an in-off the next player plays from anywhere in the D.
snooker.q5: How do I nominate a colour?
snooker.a5: After a red the game treats the first colour your cue ball hits as the one you nominated, so you never need to say it out loud. Pot that colour to score its value; potting a different colour is a foul.
snooker.a6: The same game with six reds instead of fifteen, so a frame takes a few minutes. It is popular for quick matches and is a good way to practise your break-building and the colour clearance.
snooker.q7: Can I practise without the aim line?
snooker.a7: Yes. Aim help can show the full predicted paths of every ball, just the cue line with the ghost ball, or nothing but the cue, like a real table. Solo practice adds drills (the long pot, blue to the middle, the colours clearance), undo and moving balls by hand.
snooker.a8: There is no miss rule and no free ball, and after a foul your opponent always plays on rather than asking you to play again. Colours are nominated by the first colour you hit. Scoring, foul values, re-spotting, the colours in order and the re-spotted black on a tie follow the official rules.
snooker.q9: Can I play on my phone?
snooker.a9: Yes. Drag on the table to aim, use ⟲ ⟳ for big turns and ‹ › for small ones, then the power slider and Shoot. Top view fits the long table onto a narrow screen, and full screen gives you the most room. Settings stay in this browser and nothing is sent anywhere.

snooker.lead: Play a frame of snooker in three steps.
snooker.s1b: Choose 15 or 6 reds and play the computer, a friend or solo practice with drills. Press Play.
snooker.s2b: Drag the cue ball inside the D, aim at the side of the reds with a little side spin and enough power to come back up the table.
snooker.s3b: Pot a red, then a colour, and keep going. Fouls give your opponent at least 4 points; clear the colours in order to finish the frame.
